title: Unsupervised learning separates rockfall and glacier-sliding precursors before the Blatten collapse
summary: Unsupervised clustering of 20 days of seismic data before the 28 May 2025 Blatten glacier collapse separated rockfall signals from events associated with basal glacier sliding. Sliding-related event counts accelerated approximately exponentially beginning about five days before collapse, with further acceleration about 1.5 days beforehand; the authors interpret this pattern as consistent with nucleation-like slip weakening.
ai_technology: Deep scattering network, independent component analysis and hierarchical clustering (unsupervised machine learning)
organization: Université Grenoble Alpes; Institut de Physique du Globe de Paris; University of Tokyo; Service des dangers naturels, Valais

evidence.tested: Unsupervised clustering of 20 days of seismic data before the 28 May 2025 Blatten glacier collapse separated rockfall signals from events associated with basal glacier sliding.
evidence.unknown: The finding is a retrospective analysis of one event, relying primarily on a single seismic station 5.3 km from the site. The authors describe the physical mechanism as consistent with nucleation and hypothesize that rockfalls contributed to instability; these interpretations require study of other events. The inferred slip-rate proxy has high absolute uncertainty, and the approach is not an operational early-warning system.
evidence.ai_role: The unsupervised representation and clustering explored continuous single-station seismic records without event templates, separating rockfall, glacier-sliding and cultural-noise signatures. This made the evolving sliding-related event population and its acceleration measurable in the 20-day record.
